summary.text: Presents the front matter of the WHO interim guidance Digital Documentation of COVID-19 Certificates: Vaccination Status (DDCC:VS) — Technical Specifications and Implementation Guidance (27 August 2021, WHO/2019-nCoV/Digital_certificates/vaccination/2021.1), including copyright and licensing notices, the table of contents, acknowledgements, abbreviations, a glossary of technical and data-protection terms, and the Executive Summary. The Executive Summary defines the DDCC:VS as a digitally signed HL7 FHIR representation of COVID-19 vaccination events supporting two primary scenarios (Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination) across paper and digital formats without requiring a smartphone, and outlines the minimum policy, data, and service requirements (including Health Certificate Identifiers, a Generation Service, and a Registry Service).

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by the severe acute respiratory 
syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), was first identified in December 
2019 and has spread to become a global pandemic. The outbreak has 
forced curtailment of movement, curfews and adoption of preventative 
measures to try to halt transmission, lower the burden on health 
systems, and reduce morbidity and loss of life. COVID-19 vaccines 
are being delivered at record speed, and countries need a way to 
give individuals a record of their vaccination status. Ideally, digital 
technology can be leveraged to facilitate large-

summary.text: Introduces Section 1 by framing the global COVID-19 pandemic context and the need for countries to provide verifiable records of COVID-19 vaccination status that augment fraud- and loss-prone paper cards while respecting human rights, equity, ethical considerations, and data protection principles.

blocks.title: Purpose of this document
blocks.content:
This document lays out an approach for creating a signed digital version of a vaccination record for 
COVID-19 based on a core data set of key information to be recorded, and an approach for the digital 
signature. The document leverages existing free and open standards, and is driven by the ethics, 
use cases and requirements for Digital Documentation of COVID-19 Certificates: Vaccination Status 
(DDCC:VS).

blocks.title: Target audience
blocks.content:
The primary target audience of this document is national authorities tasked with creating or 
overseeing the development of a digital vaccination certificate solution for COVID-19. The document 
may also be useful to government partners such as local businesses, international organizations, non-
governmental organizations and trade associations, that may be required to support Member States in 
developing or deploying a DDCC:VS solution.

summary.text: Identifies the primary target audience in Section 1.2 as national authorities responsible for creating or overseeing COVID-19 digital vaccination certificate solutions, along with supporting government partners, international organizations, NGOs, local businesses, and trade associations.

blocks.title: Scope
blocks.content:
1.3.1.	In scope
This document specifically focuses on how to digitally document COVID-19 vaccination status and 
attest that an individual has received a vaccine (i.e. how to provide a signed digital vaccination 
certificate). Two priority scenarios are described in Table 1: Continuity of Care and Proof of 
Vaccination. This document describes a specification for a signed digital vaccination certificate, 
including:
	
→ethical and legal considerations, and privacy and data protection principles for the design, 
implementation and use of a DDCC:VS;
	
→use cases arising from the two scenarios fo

summary.text: Defines the in-scope and out-of-scope boundaries in Section 1.3: in-scope elements cover ethical and data-protection principles, Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination use cases, the core data set, the HL7 FHIR implementation guide, and national trust framework considerations, whereas SARS-CoV-2 test and infection/recovery certificates, immunity-passport policy decisions, AEFI reporting, rollout monitoring, country-specific 2D barcode identity-binding algorithms, and selective disclosure functionality are out of scope.

blocks.title: Assumptions
blocks.content:
The technological specification for a DDCC:VS is intended to be flexible and adaptable for each Member 
State to meet its diverse public health needs as well as the diverse needs of individuals around the 
world. It is assumed that there is no one-size-fits-all solution, and so the specification must remain 
flexible and software-agnostic, while minimizing the amount of digital infrastructure required. 
The requirements outlined are intended to allow for DDCC:VS solutions to meet the needs of a 
country’s holistic public health preparedness and response plan, while still being usable in other

summary.text: Outlines the foundational assumptions in Section 1.4 regarding Member States' responsibilities in setting up and operating a DDCC:VS solution, including legal and human-rights compliance, preventing digital exclusion via paper-and-barcode support indexed by a Health Certificate Identifier (HCID), establishing a national Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) with root and document signer certificates (DSCs) not tied to individual health workers, and operating DDCC:VS Generation, Registry, and optional Repository services.

blocks.title: Methods
blocks.content:
Since the COVID-19 pandemic began, and as vaccines have shown signs of efficacy, the number 
of digital solutions for vaccination certificates has increased. For the WHO to remain software-
agnostic, the Smart Vaccination Certificate Working Group was created, with the intention of being 
a multisectoral working group focused on supporting development of key standards for digital 
vaccination certificates, sharing joint learnings, and supporting development of a governance model 
with a national trust framework architecture to support the roll-out of COVID-19 vaccines nationally (5). 
Furtherm

summary.text: Describes the methods in Section 1.5 used to develop the guidance, highlighting the creation of the multisectoral Smart Vaccination Certificate Working Group and consultations with WHO Member States and partner organizations to ensure software-agnostic, globally implementable standards.

blocks.content:

summary.text: Lists related and baseline WHO guidance documents in Section 1.6 covering risk-based international travel, public health and social measures (PHSMs), International Health Regulations (2005) Emergency Committee statements, COVID-19 vaccination monitoring, home-based immunization records, and national vaccine deployment plans.

blocks.title: Other initiatives
blocks.content:
DDCC:VS core data set guidance laid out in this document may be leveraged to generate artefacts 
conformant with other initiatives such as the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) 
Guidelines on visible digital seals (“VDS-NC”) for travel-related health proofs (16) and the European 
Union (EU) EU Digital COVID Certificate (17). Additional technical details can be found on the DDCC 
vaccination certificate implementation guide available at: WorldHealthOrganization.github.io/ddcc.

blocks.title: Ethical considerations and data protection principles
blocks.content:
SECTION 2
As with any digital solution, there are ethical considerations, such 
as potential impacts on equity and on equitable access, and data 
protection principles that need to inform the design of the technical 
specifications, as well as provide guidance on how resulting solutions 
can be ethically implemented. The following sections discuss some key 
ethical considerations and data protection principles that Member 
States are encouraged to – and, where they have legal obligations, must 
– include in their respective deployments of any DDCC:VS. These ethical 
considerations and data pro

summary.text: Introduces Section 2 by emphasizing that ethical considerations—such as equity and equitable access—and data protection principles must inform both the technical design criteria and national deployments of any DDCC:VS solution.

blocks.title: Ethical considerations for a DDCC:VS
blocks.content:
This section presents ethical considerations to take into account when designing, developing and 
deploying a DDCC:VS as part of the response to the COVID-19 pandemic (which may be extended to 
other diseases). This document covers two priority scenarios of use for a DDCC:VS, which are: 
1.	
as a record to serve as the basis for continuing healthcare for that individual (Continuity of Care); 
and
2.	
as a record documenting that an individual has received a vaccination (Proof of Vaccination).
This section therefore focuses on the ethical considerations relevant to these two use cases in a 
nat

summary.text: Details the ethical considerations for designing and deploying a DDCC:VS in Section 2.1, examining public health objectives (promoting welfare, preventing health inequities and digital exclusion, and maintaining public trust), procedural values (transparency, inclusiveness, accountability, and responsiveness), ethical risks of 'health pass' uses amid scientific uncertainties and unequal vaccine access, and six core recommendations for domestic implementation.

blocks.title: Data protection principles for a DDCC:VS
blocks.content:
This section presents fundamental data protection principles for the DDCC:VS as a prerequisite 
for continuity of care and proof of vaccination. The principles are designed to provide guidance to 
the national authorities tasked with creating or overseeing the development of the DDCC:VS. The 
objectives are to encourage Member States to adopt or adapt their national laws and regulations, as 
necessary, respect personal data protection principles, and ensure respect for the human rights and 
fundamental freedoms of individuals, in particular the right to privacy, in order to build trust in the

summary.text: Establishes seven fundamental data protection principles for DDCC:VS in Section 2.2 to guide national authorities and safeguard privacy and human rights: lawful basis, legitimate use and fair processing; transparency; purpose limitation and specification; proportionality, necessity and data minimization; confidentiality and security (including breach notification); data subject rights, complaint and legal redress; and independent oversight and accountability.

blocks.content:

State’s vaccine delivery plan. 
2.	 DATA ENTRY SITE: where the vaccination record is digitized. The record can be digitized at the care 
site if the digital solution is available, or it can be done retroactively under the auspices of the 
public health authority or health servic

2.	 A Vaccinator administers a COVID-19 vaccination.

blocks.content:
For the Proof of Vaccination scenario, there is one additional setting to consider: the verification

by the Member State. The relevant policies, including data protection policies, should be put in place 
accordingly.

all of these digital services will have a user interface that the key

section. This PKI supports the sharing of public keys that correspond to the private keys that have 
been used to cryptographically sign DDCC:VS and may support the sharing of public keys from trusted

summary.text: Introduces Section 5 on the DDCC:VS core data set, explaining that it comprises the critical Subject of Care and vaccination-event data elements required for interoperability across the Continuity of Care and Proof of Vaccination scenarios, either used directly or mapped from existing terminologies, with a full data dictionary provided in Web Annex A.

blocks.title: Core data set principles
blocks.content:
To develop the core data set, data requirements under the International Health Regulations (15), WHO 
home-based records guidance (13), WHO adverse events following immunization (AEFI) reporting 
requirements (26) and WHO immunization programme monitoring guidance are considered (12). 
The core data set has been further informed by analysis of existing digital vaccination certificates 
deployed in some countries and by pre-existing standards for digital vaccination certificates.
The following key principles were used to guide the formulation of the core data set.
	
→DATA MINIMIZATION. Aligned

summary.text: Outlines the core data set principles in Section 5.1—data minimization, open standards, implementability on both paper and digital formats, and integration with broader immunization information systems (EIRs, DHIS2, Vigiflow)—and recommends HL7 FHIR (based on the International Patient Summary) and ICD-11 as the preferred open standard and terminology system, with ICD-10, ATC, and SNOMED CT GPS mappings supported.

blocks.title: Core data elements
blocks.content:
The three key sections of the core data set are: 
1.	
the header 
2.	
data elements for each vaccination event 
3.	
vaccination certificate metadata.
The header section data elements include the Subject of Care’s ID information (see Table 10). The 
header section is intended to capture information about the vaccinated individual to allow for 
information on the vaccination event to be linked to a specific person. This data should remain the 
same regardless of which vaccination a person has received; thus, it should only be collected once.

It also introduces Section 6 on the National Trust Architecture and PKI chain of trust (Figure 13) for signing and verifying a DDCC:VS.

blocks.title: Signing a DDCC:VS
blocks.content:
The process of signing a DDCC:VS is shown in the top row of Fig. 13 and involves three steps.
1.	 The PHA generates a private and public key pair that serve as the “root certificate”. The private 
key is kept highly secure (never revealed to another party, maintained in a disconnected location, 
stored on media that is itself password-protected, etc.); the public key will be widely disseminated.
2.	 The PHA generates one or more DSC key pairs. DSC private keys are kept highly secure, and public 
keys are widely disseminated. The DSC key pair is digitally signed by the root certificate’s privat

summary.text: Explains the three-step process for digitally signing a DDCC:VS in Section 6.1 (illustrated in Figure 14): generating a root certificate key pair, signing Document Signer Certificate (DSC) key pairs with the root private key, and hashing the vaccination data and signing the document hash with the DSC private key.

blocks.title: Verifying a DDCC:VS signature
blocks.content:
The verification process, shown in in the bottom row of Fig. 13 and further detailed in Fig. 15, reverses 
the signing process to verify content in the signed DDCC:VS.
1.	 A Verifier calculates its own hash (i.e. “calculated hash”) from the information in the DDCC:VS 
using the same hashing algorithm as was used by the document signer. 
2.	 The DDCC:VS’s signed hash is read by a digital solution.
3.	 The document signer’s public key is used to cryptographically transform the signed hash back to 
the document hash. The Verifier can compare the document hash from step 2 to its own calculated 
ha

summary.text: Describes the four-step process for verifying a DDCC:VS digital signature in Section 6.2 (illustrated in Figure 15), where a Verifier computes the document hash, reads the signed hash, decrypts it using the DSC public key to confirm data integrity and signer authenticity, and validates the DSC signature using the PHA's root certificate public key.

blocks.title: Trusting a DDCC:VS signature
blocks.content:
The cryptographic strength of private–public key pairs is based on the mathematics of asymmetric 
cryptography, a process involving “one-way” mathematical functions, which are operations that are 
easy to compute in one direction but extremely hard to reverse. They provide a high level of security 
provided the private key is not compromised and remains available only to the entity performing 
the signing. Operationally, private keys are kept highly secure and public keys are broadly shared. 
Provided that a private key is not compromised and unintentionally revealed to another party, content

summary.text: Explains the mathematical and operational basis for trusting a DDCC:VS signature in Section 6.3, noting how asymmetric cryptography guarantees authenticity and non-repudiation while PKI provides trusted public-key distribution and key revocation mechanisms.

to govern the complex and dynamic health policy for implementing 
DDCC:VS should be tailored to meet the Member State’s needs, which 
vary. This section provides an overview of some key governance 
considerations for Member States implementing DDCC:VS solutions. 
However, i

summary.text: Outlines national governance considerations in Section 7 for operating a DDCC:VS trust framework at the PHA and Member State levels, comparing Root Certificate Authority and Master List approaches for sharing authorized DSCs and specifying policy requirements for certificate issuance, verification rules, revocation and remedy procedures, and cross-border data management and privacy protection.

blocks.title: Implementation considerations
blocks.content:
SECTION
Implementation 
considerations 
8 
Since COVID-19 was declared a Public Health Emergency of 
International Concern under the IHR in January 2020, there has been a 
clear and urgent need for all Member States to effectively address the 
COVID-19 pandemic. In the digital age, there has also been immediate 
acknowledgement that digital health solutions can effectively and 
immediately be leveraged to support the public health response to 
the pandemic (35). However, there are two distinct approaches that 
Member States can use to pursue the implementation of DDCC:VS, both 
of which have d

summary.text: Introduces Section 8 on implementation considerations, contrasting two strategic approaches for Member States: deploying a short-term DDCC:VS solution with a defined sunset roadmap for the COVID-19 emergency versus building a long-term digital vaccination certificate infrastructure that supports routine immunization records and broader digital health initiatives.

blocks.title: Considerations before deploying
blocks.content:
Using the framework of essential components of a digital health implementation presented in 
the WHO/ITU’s National eHealth Strategy Toolkit (36), and the guidance provided in the Digital 
implementation investment guide (DIIG) (37), the following considerations and key questions should 
be examined prior to deployment of a DDCC:VS solution.
STRATEGY AND INVESTMENT
	
→Is the DDCC:VS solution intended to be a short-term solution or a long-term digital vaccination 
certificate solution? 
	
→What are the potential benefits, risks and costs of implementing a DDCC:VS solution? These should 
be asse

summary.text: Provides pre-deployment checklists and key questions in Section 8.1 organized by the WHO/ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit and Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG) components: strategy and investment, infrastructure, legislation/policy/compliance, leadership and governance, workforce, services and applications, standards and interoperability, and evolving health content.

blocks.title: Key factors to consider with solution developers
blocks.content:
If a PHA that is responsible for the delivery of a digital solution does not have the appropriate 
technology skills in-house, then it may want to look for one or more partners to provide that service. 
The choice of a digital partner will ideally be subject to a competitive process. Multiple potential 
suppliers will be considered to identify partners that represent the best fit for the work at the optimal 
price, with consideration of the total cost of ownership, timeline and sustainability of the solution. The 
approach to inviting tenders for the work, assessing tenders, awarding a contrac

summary.text: Details key factors for Public Health Authorities to consider when procuring and partnering with external solution developers in Section 8.2, including clear terms of reference, fixed-price versus time-and-materials contracts, realistic phased timelines, single supplier versus consortium models, measurable KPIs, supplier expertise and project management track records, communication and cultural alignment, long-term partnership potential, and intellectual property and software licensing rights.

blocks.title: Cost category considerations
blocks.content:
Regardless of whether the intended DDCC:VS solution will be a short-term solution or a long-term 
digital vaccination certificate solution, specific cost categories and related cost drivers will affect 
the budget for this work. However, whether they will be incurred as a sunk cost of the pandemic (for 
short-term solutions) or an investment for future digital health systems (long-term solutions) will 
depend on the Member State’s implementation strategy. Table 13 provides a non-exhaustive list of 
possible cost drivers for implementing a DDCC:VS solution.

summary.text: Examines cost categories and budget drivers for short- and long-term DDCC:VS implementations in Section 8.3, presenting Table 13 across six lifecycle phases: ongoing governance and staffing, development and technology setup, deployment (hardware, testing, training, roll-out, and outreach), integration and interoperability, scaling (printing, human resources, IT licensing, and IT scalability), and sustained operations.

blocks.title: Additional resources to support implementation
blocks.content:
Additional resources that can be leveraged to support the implementation of DDCC:VS include 
examples of implementations already deployed, additional technical specifications for specific use 
cases, and general guidance on implementing digital health solutions. Note that the following is a non-
exhaustive list of examples. WHO will be documenting in a clearinghouse software solutions that are 
consistent with the DDCC:VS specifications.
WHO INTEROPERABILITY STANDARD FOR DDCC:VS 
	
→
DDCC:VS HL7 FHIR Implementation Guide
	
→
DDCC:VS core data dictionary, 27 July 2021
EXAMPLE DDCC:VS IMPLEMENTA

summary.text: Lists additional resources to support DDCC:VS implementation in Section 8.4, including the WHO DDCC:VS HL7 FHIR Implementation Guide and core data dictionary, example implementations and compatible software (EU Digital COVID Certificate and Gateway, OpenSRP FHIR Core, India's DIVOC, OpenHIE DDCC Transactions Mediator), ICAO VDS-NC and OpenHIE specifications, the WHO DIIG, and WHO international travel guidance.

blocks.title: Guiding principles for mapping the WHO Family of International Classifications (WHO-FIC) and other classifications
blocks.content:
International Classifications (WHO-FIC) and other 
classifications
Mapping from classifications and terminologies used in existing systems to the International 
Classification of Diseases, 11th revision (ICD-11), and other WHO-FIC classifications should follow the 
principles listed below.1 
1.	
Establish use case(s) prior to developing the map – this involves identifying and formulating the 
purpose(s) for which the map will be used and describing the different types of users and how 
they will process data using the map. 
2.	
Clearly define the purpose, scope and directionality of the map.
3

summary.text: Presents Annex 3, setting out 15 guiding principles for mapping existing classifications and terminologies to ICD-11 and other WHO Family of International Classifications (WHO-FIC) standards, covering use-case definition, unidirectional single-purpose maps, transparent documentation, producer involvement, quality assurance and gold-standard usage validation, versioning and maintenance, manual and computational mapping workflows, equivalence and cardinality definitions, machine-readability, and mapping to the ICD-11 foundation component.

blocks.title: What is public key infrastructure (PKI)?
blocks.content:
The solution discussed in this document involves applying digital signatures to information to provide 
a guarantee that the information has been validated by an accredited authority. The proposed method 
is to employ a digital certificate using a private–public key pair, a common mathematical approach 
for encryption and digital trust. The processes, systems, software and rules around the management 
of these certificates form a PKI – essentially, all the components that need to be in place for a trusted 
solution to work.
WHY IS A PKI NEEDED?

summary.text: Presents Annex 5 (Table A5.1), specifying 64 generic non-functional requirements (`DDCC.NFXNREQ.001` through `DDCC.NFXNREQ.064`) for DDCC:VS digital solutions across 11 categories: accessibility, availability (SLAs), current and forecast capacity, disaster recovery/business continuity/resilience, performance/response time, security and privacy, regulation and compliance, reliability, horizontal and vertical scalability, supportability, usability, and data retention/archiving.

blocks.title: Open Health Information Exchange (OpenHIE)-based architectural blueprint
blocks.content:
architectural blueprint
This section illustrates how a standards-based health-data-sharing infrastructure could support point-
of-care digital health solutions. If digital health solutions are employed in real time during the vaccine 
administration event, it is anticipated that complementary digital health infrastructure, such as the 
architectural elements described by the OpenHIE specification, could be leveraged.

summary.text: Presents Annex 6, illustrating an Open Health Information Exchange (OpenHIE)-based architectural blueprint (Figure A6.1) for point-of-care DDCC:VS issuance and describing how OpenHIE registries and repositories—Terminology Services, Client Registry, Facility Registry, Health Worker Registry, Product Catalogue, and Shared Health Record (SHR)—supply and persist DDCC:VS core data elements.
